t: Decode XORed Permutation — Recovering the Anchor from XOR of 1..n
o:
Same encoding as LC 1720 — `encoded[i] = perm[i] XOR perm[i+1]` — but this time the first element is NOT given. Instead we know perm is a permutation of 1..n and, crucially, that n is odd.
That oddness is the crux. XOR-ing the entries `encoded[1], encoded[3], encoded[5], ...` expands to (perm[1]^perm[2]) ^ (perm[3]^perm[4]) ^ ..., because there are n − 1 (an even count) terms split perfectly into adjacent pairs. So that running value equals perm[1] ^ perm[2] ^ ... ^ perm[n−1] — every element except perm[0], each appearing exactly once.
Meanwhile T = 1 XOR 2 XOR ... XOR n is computable directly, and by definition it equals perm[0] XOR (that same odd-index sum). Therefore perm[0] = T XOR (encoded[1] ^ encoded[3] ^ ...). Example 1: T = 1^2^3 = 0 and the odd sum is 1, so perm[0] = 1; chaining then gives [1,2,3]. Example 2: T = 1^...^5 = 1, odd sum = 5^6 = 3, anchor 2, chain rebuilds [2,4,1,5,3]. With n up to 10^5 the reconstruction must be linear — a try-every-starting-value search is quadratic and too slow, but it nicely explains why the answer is unique.
k: XOR of the complete range 1..n acts as a global checksum that substitutes for the missing first element.
Because n is odd, XOR-ing encoded at odd indices covers every permutation element except perm[0] exactly once.
Once perm[0] is anchored, chained decoding finishes exactly as in the easier sibling problem.

a.n: Approach 1: Try Every Candidate First Element
a.i: Without first, guess it: for each candidate c in 1..n, run the ordinary chained decode starting from c and validate that the result is a permutation of 1..n — every value in range and seen exactly once. Exactly one candidate survives, which also demonstrates uniqueness. Validation aborts early on any violation, but the overall cost is still quadratic: instructive to explain, too slow when n approaches 10^5.
s: For each candidate c from 1 to n:
Chain-decode starting from c, aborting early if a produced value is 0, exceeds n, or repeats.
Return the first candidate that yields a full valid permutation.
a.t: O(n^2) — up to n candidates, each decoded and validated in O(n); too slow at the largest constraint.
a.sp: O(n) — the trial permutation plus seen flags.

a.n: Approach 2: Checksum Anchor Plus Linear Sweep
a.i: Compute T = 1 XOR 2 XOR ... XOR n with a simple loop. Compute O = XOR of encoded at odd indices; by the pairing argument above this equals perm[1] XOR ... XOR perm[n−1]. Since T = perm[0] XOR O, the missing anchor is perm[0] = T XOR O, after which one sweep rebuilds everything exactly like the easy version.
s: XOR encoded entries at odd indices into oddSum.
Extend with perm[i+1] = perm[i] XOR encoded[i] and return perm.
a.t: O(n) — three linear passes over data of size n.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary beyond the O(n) output array.

w: Lead with the checksum anchor — deriving it aloud (odd n pairs the encoded terms perfectly, leaving perm[0] exposed) is the real test here; mention the brute force only to argue uniqueness. Pitfalls: pairing even-indexed encoded entries by mistake (they leave two elements unpaired), assuming the trick survives even n (it does not — several permutations share one encoding), and off-by-one slips in the rebuild loop. Edge cases: smallest input n = 3. Follow-ups: construct two distinct permutations of an even-sized range with identical encodings to show why parity matters, or decode when the mixing operation is addition.
